summary: Choosing and running Meta, TikTok and native traffic for COD nutra within their health rules, and tracking every lead from click to approved status with click IDs and postbacks. You finish with a rule card that handles the delay before approvals arrive.

objectives: By the end you can compare Meta, TikTok, native and other sources for COD nutra.

steps.h: Why: the source decides cost, buyer and risk
steps.p: Your traffic source sets what you pay for attention, what kind of buyer you reach and how strict the rules are. Picking a source the offer does not allow, or one whose health rules you have not read, can waste a whole test budget or close an account in a day.

d.b: Pick the source before the creative
d.s: Allowed by the offer, allowed by the platform, affordable for your test.

steps.say: Here's why the source comes first. Your traffic source sets what you pay for attention, what kind of buyer you reach, and how strict the rules are. Pick a source the offer doesn't allow, or one whose health rules you haven't read, and you can waste a whole test budget, or close an account in a day. So the order is on screen: pick the source before the creative. It must be allowed by the offer, allowed by the platform, and affordable for your test.

steps.say: These cards show the sources most nutra affiliates use for C O D, cash on delivery, offers. Meta, Facebook and Instagram, has broad reach, with strict health and personal-attribute rules. TikTok skews younger, is video-first, and is strict on weight and health claims. Native networks place ads on news and content sites, and suit advertorials. Google and YouTube bring high intent, but are very strict on health claims. Push and pop are cheap, but often low intent and high trash. And creators bring trust, but need disclosure and approved claims. Every one of these rules changes, so read the current policy.

steps.h: Example: cost per approved by source
steps.p: Example: the same offer on two sources. Meta has a higher click cost but a better lead rate and approval. Native has cheap clicks but buyers who read less carefully. The cheaper click does not win here. These figures are illustrative; test your own.
steps.more: Maths: Meta CPC $0.20 (a $3 CPM at 1.5% CTR: $3 ÷ 15 clicks per 1,000 impressions). CPL = $0.20 ÷ 0.06 = $3.33. Cost per approved = $3.33 ÷ 0.45 = $7.41. Native CPL = $0.08 ÷ 0.025 = $3.20, then ÷ 0.38 = $8.42. Both are under the $10.50 target in this Example; Meta also passes the $8.40 scale line.
steps.say: Here's the same offer on two sources. Illustrative figures. Meta costs twenty cents a click, native just eight cents. But Meta's lead rate is six percent against two and a half. Cost per approved lead ends up seven forty one on Meta, and eight forty two on native. Both are under the ten fifty target in this example, but the cheaper click doesn't win. Test your own.

steps.h: From click cost to cost per approved
steps.p: Use this chain for any source. It lets you compare sources that are sold differently, by CPM or by CPC, on the one number that matters. You will need real test data to fill it, so treat your first guesses as rough.
d: CPC
Lead rate
Approval
Cost per approved
steps.say: This is the chain you'll use for any source. C P C, cost per click, divided by lead rate, divided by approval rate, equals cost per approved lead. Why does that help? Because some sources sell by the thousand impressions and some by the click, and this brings them all to the one number that matters. You need real test data to fill it in, so treat your first guesses as rough.

steps.h: Why: Meta finds who you ask for
steps.p: Meta's delivery system looks for people likely to do the event you optimise for. If you optimise for form fills, it finds form fillers, including careless ones. If you can send approved orders back, it can learn to find buyers. The event you choose matters as much as the creative.

d.b: You get the event you optimise for
d.s: Leads are easy to get. Approved leads are what pay.

steps.say: Here's the key idea. Meta's delivery system looks for people likely to do the event you optimise for. Optimise for form fills, and it finds form fillers, including careless ones. But if you can send approved orders back, it can learn to find buyers. As the screen says, you get the event you optimise for. Leads are easy to get. Approved leads are what pay.

steps.p: Meta's guidance has long been that an ad set needs around 50 optimisation events a week to leave the learning phase. We are not certain the figure is current; check Meta's Help Center. Here is what that means for each event.

objectives: By the end you can project approved leads while statuses are still pending.

steps.p: On day one an ad set may show nine leads and two approvals. It looks like $18 per approved and you want to kill it. Two days later it has four approvals and $9 per approved. COD rules must account for lag, or you kill winners and keep losers.

d.s: Use projections to kill, never to scale.

steps.say: Here's the trap. On day one, an ad set shows nine leads and two approvals. It looks like eighteen dollars per approved, and you want to kill it. Two days later, it has four approvals, and nine dollars per approved. C O D, cash on delivery, rules must account for that lag, or you kill winners and keep losers. Judge statuses after they land. Use projections to kill, never to scale.

steps.p: While statuses are pending, multiply leads by your expected approval rate to estimate approved leads. Divide spend by that. Use your network's average or your own recent average for the geo, whichever is lower.
d: Spend

steps.say: While statuses are pending, you can project. Look at the equation. Spend, divided by leads times expected approval, equals projected cost per approved. For expected approval, use your network's average or your own recent average for the geo, whichever is lower. Choosing the lower one keeps the projection from flattering you.

steps.h: Example: actual vs projected on day 1
steps.p: Example: $36 spend, 9 leads, 2 approved so far, 5 pending, 2 rejected. Actual cost per approved looks like $18, past the $14 kill line. Projected, using 45% expected approval, it is $8.89. The real answer will be somewhere between, so you wait for statuses.
steps.more: Maths: 9 × 0.45 = 4.05 projected approved. $36 ÷ 4.05 = $8.89. Two days later 4 are approved: $36 ÷ 4 = $9.00. That is under the $10.50 target, above the $8.40 scale line, so keep. Killing on day one would have thrown away a decent ad set.
steps.say: Let's see it on day one. Example figures. Thirty six dollars spend, nine leads, two approved so far, five pending, two rejected. In the table, actual so far is two approved, eighteen dollars each, past the fourteen dollar kill line. Projected, using forty five percent expected approval, is about four approved, eight eighty nine each. And after statuses land, it's four approved at nine dollars. That's under the ten fifty target, so keep. Killing on day one would have thrown away a decent ad set.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt, built on the Foundations rule card with payout $14 and target $10.50. Projections assume average approval, which is generous; if even the generous view fails, kill. Never scale on a projection.
steps.say: Here's the C O D rule card, built on payout fourteen dollars and target ten fifty. Zero-lead kill, twenty one or more spent, no leads. Projected kill, thirty one fifty spent, projected over fourteen. Actual kill, ninety percent final, thirty one fifty spent, actual over fourteen. Keep, actual eight forty to fourteen, budget flat. Scale, actual eight forty or under with three plus approved, twenty percent every forty eight hours or more. Otherwise, hold. Projections assume average approval, which is generous. If even that fails, kill. Never scale on a projection.

Note a case where the two lines differ: at $15 per approved after $31.50, our card kills (above $14) while a 1.5 × target card would hold. Our card is stricter because the payout is $14.

steps.h: Report by lead date, not status date
steps.p: Example: always group results by the day the lead came in. If you count approvals on the day they arrive, Monday's approvals land on Tuesday's row and every day looks wrong. Lead-date cohorts keep spend and results together.
steps.more: Read it like this: Monday and Tuesday are ready to judge. Monday is $60 ÷ 7 = $8.57, Tuesday $60 ÷ 6 = $10.00. Wednesday and Thursday are not ready; their low approvals are mostly lag. Projected for Thursday: 15 × 0.45 = 6.75, $60 ÷ 6.75 = $8.89.
steps.say: Always group results by the day the lead came in. If you count approvals on the day they arrive, Monday's approvals land on Tuesday's row, and every day looks wrong. Look at the example. Monday, sixty dollars, seven approved, a hundred percent final. Tuesday, six approved, ninety two percent final. Those two are ready to judge. Wednesday has three approved at forty percent final, and Thursday one approved at ten percent. Their low approvals are mostly lag, not failure.

steps.p: Each morning, update one row per ad set. Statuses-final percentage decides which column you use. Then write the decision and the reason. It takes ten minutes and stops emotional decisions.

No; around 50 a week needs about $75 a day, so optimise for Lead and judge on approved

exam.why: $33 ÷ 1 = $33 per approved, over $14 after spend past 3 × target.

A different sub map per campaign

Both: a cure-type claim and an undisclosed paid promotion

exam.q: An ad set has 95% statuses final, $50 spend, 7 approved. Decision?
exam.why: $50 ÷ 7 = $7.14, under the $8.40 scale line with more than 3 approved.

exam.q: Tracker revenue for last week is $980, network revenue is $1,120. What do you do?

exam.q: Why does the COD rule card allow kills on projections but not scales?
options: Projections use average approval, which is generous; if even that fails, the ad set is bad, but a good projection is not yet proof
exam.why: A generous estimate that still fails is a safe kill. Scaling risks real money, so it waits for actual approvals.
